5.80.m: Pārvatī said: / When the terrible Kali yuga has arrived, crowded with the crocodiles of sensory objects, / how can that be maintained by those afflicted with children, wife, wealth, and the like, O Lord?
Tell the means for that, O Mahādeva, treasure of mercy! / The Lord said: / The name of Hari, the name of Hari, the name of Hari alone!
‘Hare Rāma, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa’—which is auspicious— / Kali does not afflict those who constantly speak thus.
Doing work from time to time, one should also remember the names, / saying repeatedly, ‘Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa.’
Combining my name and your name interchangeably, / even he would be freed from sin, as fire [burns] a heap of cotton.
Beginning with 'Jaya', or else preceded by the word 'Śrī', / repeating that auspicious name of mine, one is freed from sin.
By day, by night, and at twilight—at all times one should remember it. / Remembering Rāma day and night, one sees Kṛṣṇa with one's own eyes.
Whether impure or pure, at all times and ever, / from the mere recollection of the name, one is freed from worldly existence in an instant.
Even of one laden with various offenses, the name destroys the sin. / Sacrifice, vow, austerity, and gifting are not complete in the Kali yuga;
bathing in the Gaṅgā and the name of Hari—these two are unfailing.
A myriad murders, a thousand fierce sins, and intercourse with a crore of wives of one's teacher, / and other thefts do not remain, O auspicious one, through the name of Govinda, dear to Hari.
Whether impure or pure, or in whatever condition one may be, / whoever remembers the lotus-eyed one is clean both externally and internally.
From the mere recollection of the name and likewise from contemplating its meaning, / having made [an image] of gold, silver, or of flour in the shape of a garland,
marked upon the feet, one should indeed begin the worship. / He who bears the discus at the base of the big toe of the right foot,
for cutting off the transmigration of the person bowed down there— / and at the base of the middle toe Acyuta bears a lotus,
most beautiful, to entice the black-bee minds of meditators; / below the lotus he bears a flag, a flag of victory over all misfortunes.
From the base of the little toe [he bears] the thunderbolt, cleaving the mass of sins of devotees; / in the middle of the side [he bears] the goad, causing delight to the hearts of devotees.
On the joint of the big toe he bears the barley corn, full of the abundance of enjoyment; / and at the heel the mace, shattering the mountain of sins of all embodied beings.
That unborn Lord bears [them] for the manifestation of all knowledge. / The marks such as the lotus that are again on the right,
and those which dwell on the left foot, that ocean of compassion bears. / Therefore, the glorification of Govinda, delightful with the rasa of bliss,
one should hear and ever recite; he is liberated, there is no doubt. / I shall declare the duty of each month, supremely pleasing to Viṣṇu.
In Jyeṣṭha, being pure, one should carefully perform the bathing of Śrī Viṣṇu. / Sins committed daily, in a fortnight, in a month, in a season, or in a year,
thousands of murders of Brahmins, committed knowingly or unknowingly, / and myriads of thefts of gold, drinking of liquor, and violating the teacher's bed,
and whatever thousands of crores of minor sins there are— / all of them are destroyed on the day of the full moon.
Then one should sprinkle that pitcher-water upon the head of Acyuta / with the mantra of the Puruṣasūkta and with the Pāvamānī verses,
with coconut water, and likewise with palm-fruit water, / with jewel-infused water, with perfumed water, and with flower water.
Having worshipped with the fivefold offerings according to one's wealth and means, / one should offer the sound of the bell, saying: 'Ghaṃ, obeisance to the bell!'
'For me who am fallen into the great darkness, burdened with an accumulation of sins, / protect me, a sinner, falling into the dreadful ocean of saṃsāra!'
A learned, pure Brahmin learned in the Veda who acts thus / is freed from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, one should celebrate the great festival of sleep; / in Āṣāḍha one should hold the chariot [festival], and in Śrāvaṇa the Śravaṇā rite.
In Bhādra, on his birthday, one should be intent upon fasting; / in the month of Āśvina, one should arrange the turning over of him who is asleep.
One should perform the awakening of Śrī Hari, otherwise one harms Viṣṇu; / and in the auspicious month of Āśvina, one should worship Mahāmāyā,
made of gold or silver, having the form of Viṣṇu, without animal sacrifice. / Injury and malice must not be done; the worshipper of Viṣṇu is righteous.
In the months of Kārtika and Pauṣa, one should perform meritorious acts at will; / and one should offer a lamp to Dāmodara in an elevated place.
The lamp should measure four aṅgulas, with seven wicks; / and at the end of the fortnight an auspicious row of lights should be made.
In Mārgaśīrṣa, on the sixth day of the bright fortnight, with white garments, / one should worship the Lord of the world, and especially Brahmā.
In Pauṣa [one should perform] the shower of flowers, and avoid loose sandalwood paste; / at the Saṃkrānti in the month of Māgha, from perfumed grains of rice,
one should offer food to Viṣṇu and recite this mantra. / With devotion one should feed Brahmins standing before the God of gods.
Having honoured the devotees of the Lord and the twice-born with the thought that they are the Lord, / when one devotee is fed, a crore are fed.
By the mere feeding of Brahmins, that which is defective certainly becomes complete. / On the fifth day of the bright fortnight, having bathed Keśava,
and worshipped him according to the rules, with mango sprouts, / and with various fruit-powders, perfumed and refined through cloth,
in an enchanting grove illuminated by blazing lamps, / with grapes, sugarcane, plantains, limes, oranges, and betel nuts,
with coconuts, myrobalans, jackfruits, and yellow myrobalans, / and with various fragments of trees endowed with flowers of all seasons,
and with other various fruits and flowers, / with canopies covered with flowers, and with pitchers filled with water,
adorned with branches and twigs of mango, with umbrellas and chowries, / remembering, 'Victory to Kṛṣṇa!', preceded by circumambulation.
Especially in the Kali yuga, the swing festival is prescribed / in Phālguna, on the fourteenth day, during the period called the eighth yāma,
or on the full moon day at the junction called Pratipad, / one should worship according to rule with devotion, using four kinds of red powder,
white, red, light-yellow, and deep-yellow, blended with camphor and the like, / and enchanting with colored powders through the combination with turmeric dye,
or with other color forms one should please the Supreme Lord. / Beginning on the eleventh day, one should conclude it on the fifth;
the swing festival is prescribed for five days or for three days. / Men who even once see Kṛṣṇa swinging facing the south,
having seen him, are freed from heaps of offenses; of this there is no doubt. / Having placed in a vessel of water in the month named Mādhava,
in a vessel of gold, silver, copper, or earthen, / whoever worships the god dwelling in the water, originated from the Śālagrāma,
or an image, O highly fortunate one, his merit cannot be counted. / Having performed the offering of damana, one should present it to Śrī Viṣṇu.
In Vaiśākha, Śrāvaṇa, and Bhādra, the wind-cleansing should be performed; / when the wind is in the earlier directions during rites such as damana,
it should be performed according to rule; otherwise it becomes fruitless. / In Vaiśākha, especially on the third day, in the midst of water,
or in a maṇḍala, or in a pavilion in a great forest, / one should diligently nourish his body day after day with fragrant sandalwood,
just as one would nourish a person with an emaciated body. / Sandalwood, agallochum, hrībera, black saffron, and rocanā,
spikenard, and murā—they know these as the eight perfumes of Viṣṇu. / With those various perfumes one should smear the limbs of Viṣṇu.
Ground tulasī wood combined with camphor and agallochum, / or mixed with saffron, is called haricandana.
Those mortals who with devotion see Kṛṣṇa at the time of the festival / have no return [to rebirth] even in hundreds of crores of kalpas.
Those who bathe the god of gods with waters mixed with fragrances, / or indeed should place the Lord of the universe within flowers,
having gone there to Vṛndāvana and prepared fruits, / should feed that in its entirety to a worthy devotee of Viṣṇu.
One should offer coconut fruit having extracted the seed-capsule, / and one should offer jackfruit having extracted the pulp from its casing.
One should offer rice mixed with curds, bathed in ghee; / and cakes cooked with flour, eighteen kinds [of pastries] with ghee,
and ripe fruits [cooked] with sesame oils, one should present. / Whatever is pleasing to oneself, that one should offer to the Lord.
Having offered food, garments, and the like, one must never take it back; / and whatever was given up for Viṣṇu, [let it be given] especially to his devotees.

Thus has this been spoken to you briefly, O great goddess;
it should be concealed with great effort, like one's own vulva, O Pārvatī.

If there is qualification for understanding the class of scriptures describing the form and qualities of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, what need is there for other recitations? / If the mind is truly fixed upon the neck-garlands of devotion's play in the rasa of love for him, what use indeed are desirable women?

Therefore, let people worship with their minds the Lord of the cowherd boys of Vraja, the soil of Vṛndāvana, and the waters of the Yamunā. / When the body is anointed with the dust of the lotus feet of the protector of that realm, aloes, sandalwood, and the like are utterly in vain.

5.81.m: The sages said: / Live long, O righteous Sūta! The nectar of Śrī Kṛṣṇa's deeds, / which carries devotees across existence, has all been revealed by you.
Declare, O lord, the entire daily sport of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, / by hearing which, O righteous one, devotion to Kṛṣṇa flourishes.
Tell us separately the rules and characteristics of the guru, the disciple, and the mantra, / O fortunate one, for you are our supreme friend.
Sūta said: / Once, bowing down to Sadāśiva, the teacher of the world, / seated on the bank of the Yamunā, Nārada addressed the god of gods:
Nārada said: / O god of gods, O Mahādeva, omniscient Lord of the universe, / knower of the truth of divine dharma, foremost among knowers of Kṛṣṇa's mantras!
Kṛṣṇa's mantras were obtained by me from you, and others from my father; / all of them—the king of mantras and the rest—have been mastered by me in accordance with the truth,
through many thousands of years by subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits, / consuming dried leaves, water, air, and the like, and fasting,
avoiding the sight and conversation of women, sleeping on the bare ground, / having conquered the sixfold qualities of desire and the rest, restraining the external senses.
Even when this was done, my soul was not satisfied, O Śaṅkara. / Therefore speak of that which is accomplished without purificatory rites and the like, O Lord,
which yields the highest fruit simply from being pronounced once. / If I am qualified, O Lord of gods, then tell me out of compassion.
Śiva said: / Well asked, O fortunate one, desiring the welfare of the world! / Even though it is closely guarded, I shall tell you the wish-fulfilling jewel of mantras,
the secret of secrets, the best mystery of mysteries, / which was not told by me to the goddess, nor earlier to your elder brothers.
I shall tell you the matchless couplet, the Kṛṣṇa mantra, / indeed the pair called the wish-fulfilling jewel of mantras.
The synonyms of this mantra are likewise 'the five-worded one': / the word 'gopījana', ending with 'vallabha', and then 'caraṇau' [feet],
and 'śaraṇam' [shelter] and 'prapadye' [I approach]. This consists of five words. / The wish-fulfilling jewel of mantras is declared to be a great mantra of sixteen syllables.
Having said 'namo gopījana', one should then say 'vallabhābhyām'. / This mantra consisting of two words is said to have ten syllables.
Having repeated this five-worded [mantra] even once with faith upon faith, / one certainly attains the presence of Kṛṣṇa's beloveds; there is no doubt.
There is no requirement of preliminary rites, nor of the order of rules for nyāsa; / there is no restriction of place or time, nor examination of enemy, friend, and the like.
And everyone here is eligible, right down to the Cāṇḍāla, O lord of sages: / women, Śūdras and the rest, and also the dull, the mute, and the lame,
and other Hūṇas, Kirātas, Pulindas, and Pukkasas, / Ābhīras, Yavanas, Kaṅkas, Khasas, and other low-born castes,
those intent on deceit and egotism, sinners, those devoted to slander, / slayers of cows, brāhmaṇas, and the like, those guilty of the greatest secondary sins,
those devoid of knowledge and dispassion, those excluded from hearing [the scriptures] and the like— / these and all others are eligible for this mantra,
if they possess devotion to Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of all lords; / then all are eligible, not otherwise, O best of sages.
Though one be a sacrificer, devoted to charity, a practitioner of all tantras, / truth-speaking, or an ascetic, one who has crossed over the Veda and the Vedāṅgas,
devoted to Brahman, high-born, or an ascetic intent on vows, / he is not eligible here if he is devoid of devotion to Kṛṣṇa.
Therefore, it should not be spoken to one who is not a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, to the ungrateful, to the arrogant, / nor to one lacking faith, nor to an atheist,
nor should it be told to one who does not wish to serve, nor to one who has not served for a full year. / To one with undivided devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, free from deceit and greed,
and liberated from lust and anger, this should be given with effort. / And I myself am its seer, and the Gāyatrī is said to be the metre;
the deity of the mantra is proclaimed to be the beloved of the cowherd maidens. / Its application is declared to be in the servitude of Hari along with his beloved.
One should arrange the five bodily parts with the mantras beginning with the discus and the like; / or rather, one should perform the nyāsa on the hands and limbs with its own seed-syllable.
The first syllable of the mantra, adorned on its top with an anusvāra, / 'Gam', becomes the seed-syllable; 'namaḥ' is declared here as the śakti.
The ten limbs are formed by the final syllables, and with them also worship [is performed] / with perfumes, flowers, and the like, or with water alone if these are unavailable.
It should be performed according to the previous rule of nyāsa for the satisfaction of Hari. / Hence, others declare nyāsa and the like for this mantra,
which grants the state of having accomplished one's aim simply from being pronounced once. / Even so, one should constantly apply it ten times for the sake of repetition and the like.
Now I shall declare the meditation of this mantra, O best of the twice-born: / dressed in yellow garments, dark as a raincloud, two-armed, wearing a forest garland,
wearing a crest made of peacock feathers, his face resembling ten million moons, / his eyes rolling gently, adorned with an ear-ornament of karṇikāra flowers,
bearing on his forehead a circular tilaka fashioned / on both sides with sandalwood and in the middle with a dot of saffron,
radiant with two earrings resembling the newly risen sun, / with mirror-like cheeks shining with droplets of perspiration,
his eyes resting upon the face of his beloved, his eyebrows raised in playful side-glances, / his prominent nose glistening with a pearl placed at its tip,
his lower lip like a ripe bimba fruit shining with the moonlight of his teeth, / his hands splendid with armlets, bracelets, and rings set with excellent gems,
holding a flute and the like, and likewise a lotus in his left hand, / his waist gleaming with a girdle, his feet splendid with anklets,
restless with the surge of the rasa of amorous play, his eyes darting, / laughing with his beloved, and making her laugh repeatedly.
Thus, at the foot of the wish-fulfilling tree, upon a jeweled throne / in the forest of Vṛndā, one should meditate on Kṛṣṇa seated together with his beloved.
Then one should meditate on Rādhikā standing at his left side, / clad in a blue bodice, having a brilliance equal to molten gold,
with her gently smiling lotus face half veiled by the border of her silk garment, / her eyes fixed on the face of her beloved, her restless gaze like that of a cakorī bird,
and offering with her thumb and forefinger into the lotus mouth of her beloved / areca nut accompanied by betel leaf and [lime] powder;
her firm, elevated breasts gleaming with pearl necklaces, / slender-waisted, broad-hipped, adorned with an array of tinkling bells,
wearing jeweled earrings, armlets, signet rings, and bracelets, / with ringing bangles and anklets, and jeweled toe-rings,
her captivating limbs embodying the essence of beauty, lovely in every part, / immersed in the nectar of bliss, serene, endowed with fresh youth.
And her female companions, O best of brahmins, of equal age and virtues to her, / should be imagined as devoted to her service with chowries, fans, and other things.
Now I shall tell you the meaning of the mantra; listen, O Nārada: / by the external forms of the phenomenal world, through her partial aspects such as the powers of māyā and others,

and likewise by the internal forms, the eternal manifestations such as consciousness and the rest, / because she conceals [all these], the beloved of Kṛṣṇa is called Gopī, Rādhikā; / the goddess Rādhikā is declared to be identical with Kṛṣṇa, the supreme deity.

She is the essential form of all Lakṣmīs, the embodiment of Kṛṣṇa's joy;
therefore she is proclaimed by the wise as "the delight-giving potency" (hlādinī), O brāhmaṇa.
Durgā and others consisting of the three guṇas are a fraction of tens of millions of parts of her; / she, however, is directly Mahālakṣmī, and Kṛṣṇa is the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
There is not the slightest difference between these two, O best of sages: / she is Durgā and Hari is Rudra; Kṛṣṇa is Indra and she is Śacī;
she is Sāvitrī and Hari is Brahmā; she is Dhūmorṇā and Hari is Yama. / What is the use of saying much, O best of sages? Without the two of them, nothing exists.
The entire world, characterized by the sentient and the insentient, consists of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa. / Thus know everything to be the manifestation of just those two, O Nārada.
It cannot be told by me even in hundreds of millions of years. / In the three worlds, the earth is honored; superior to that is Jambūdvīpa;
even there, Bhārata-varṣa; even there, the city of Mathurā; / there, the place named Vṛndāvana; there, the multitude of gopīs;
there, the group of Rādhā's female companions; even there, Rādhikā is superior. / Owing to the greater degree of her proximity, each successive one is superior.
Indeed, nothing else has been stated here regarding the earth and the rest: / this very Rādhikā is the cowherd woman, and the multitude of her friends is the troop of gopīs.
Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa are the beloved masters of the life-breath of that circle of her female companions; / may their feet be my refuge: here I take shelter.
I, a living being exceedingly afflicted, have come and surrendered [to them]; / I who have obtained refuge, and whatever belongs to me,
all is for them, meant for their purpose, to be enjoyed by them; I do not belong to myself, nor is anything mine. / Thus has the meaning of the mantra been told to you in brief, O brahmin.
The purpose of the couple, depositing (nyāsa), surrender (prapatti), taking refuge (śaraṇāgati), / and offering oneself (ātmārpaṇa)—these five synonymous terms have been spoken by me to you.
This alone should be contemplated day and night by those who are unwearied.

5.82.m: Śiva said: / Now I shall declare the rules for initiation; listen, O Nārada, according to truth: / merely by hearing them, one is liberated, even without the performance of the ritual.
A wise man, understanding the entire world from Brahmā downward to be perishable, / and experiencing only threefold suffering, beginning with that relating to oneself,
and because all pleasures are impermanent, O best of sages, / casting them into the category of suffering, freed from them,
having become detached, should contemplate the means for the abandonment of saṃsāra, / exceedingly delighted at the attainment of unequaled happiness.
Understanding indeed the difficulty [of the path] for men, the highly intelligent one, / greatly distressed, should then go for refuge to a guru, O brahmin.
Tranquil, free from envy, devoted to Kṛṣṇa, having no other purpose, / having no other means, glorious, free from desire and greed,
knowing the truth of the aesthetic experience of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, best among the knowers of Kṛṣṇa's mantras, / always sheltered by Kṛṣṇa's mantra, devoted to the mantra, ever pure,
an instructor in true righteousness, ever directing toward good conduct, / belonging to a lineage of transmission, full of compassion, detached—[such a one] is called a guru.
Endowed mostly with such qualities, desiring to serve at the feet of the guru, / exceedingly devoted to the guru, and a seeker of liberation—[such a one] is called a disciple.
Direct service unto Him through love, by which one becomes a devotee of the Lord, / is declared to be liberation by the wise who know the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
Having taken refuge at the feet of his guru, he should report his own conduct. / Dispelling his doubts and instructing him again and again,
to the disciple bowed at his feet, tranquil, and desirous of serving his feet, / the guru, with a very delighted mind, should impart the supreme mantra.
With sandalwood paste or with clay he should draw upon the roots of the arms, / on the left and right, O brāhmaṇa, the conch and discus in proper order.
Then he should apply the vertical mark according to rule on the forehead and other limbs; / thereafter he should impart the pair of mantras into his right ear.
And he should explain the meaning of the mantra to him properly in succession. / A name accompanied by the word 'dāsa' should carefully be given to him.
Then, with great devotion and affection, the wise [disciple] should feed the Vaiṣṇavas, / and he should also worship the venerable guru with garments, ornaments, and the like.
He should give all his wealth to the guru, or half of it, O great sage; / surrendering even their own bodies, the destitute should abide with the guru.
The wise person who is consecrated with these five sacraments / becomes a participant in the servitorship of Kṛṣṇa, and not otherwise even in crores of eons.
Branding, the vertical mark, the mantra, the conferring of a name, / and fifth, worship—these are declared as the [five] sacraments by ancient sages.
Branding is with the conch, discus, and other marks; the mark is said to be with a space in between; / the name is accompanied by the word 'dāsa'; the mantra is the one called the couplet.
Worship of the guru and the Vaiṣṇava is called sacrifice. / These supreme sacraments have been recounted by me to you.
Now I shall declare to you the duties of surrendered souls, O Nārada, / abiding by which men in the Kali age will go to the abode of Hari.
Having thus received the mantra from the guru, devoted to the worship of the guru, / serving the guru daily, the intelligent person should meditate upon his grace.
Then he should learn the duties of the virtuous, especially of the surrendered souls; / with the thought that they are his chosen deity, he should daily satisfy the Vaiṣṇavas.
Just as women in love take beating and rebuking / as objects of enjoyment, so should all things from Vaiṣṇavas be taken by the wise.
Worry regarding this world and the next should never be entertained; / this worldly [life] is always to be experienced as the result of previously performed action.
Likewise, Kṛṣṇa Himself will take care of what pertains to the next world; / therefore, human effort in that regard must be abandoned by men in every way.
Abandoning all other means, worship is to be performed with devotion toward Kṛṣṇa, / just as a woman devoted to her husband, when her beloved has long gone abroad,
affectionate toward her beloved, wretched, longing only for his company, / constantly meditates on his virtues, sings of them, and also listens to them,
so should one practice the remembrance and celebration of Śrī Kṛṣṇa's virtues, sports, and the like; / but that should never be performed again as a mere means [to an end].
Just as, on finding her beloved who has returned after a long absence abroad, looking upon him with passionate love, / kissing him, or embracing him, or drinking him in with the corner of her eyes,
she serves him with supreme joy as if having attained the bliss of Brahman, / so should one serve Hari through His revered icon-incarnation.
Always having no other refuge, and likewise having no other means; / because of having no other means and goal, he should have no other purpose.
He should not worship another deity, nor bow to him, nor remember him, / nor gaze upon him, nor sing of him, nor ever revile him.
He should not eat the leftovers of another, nor wear the remnants of another; / he should avoid conversation, obeisance, and the like with non-Vaiṣṇavas.
He should never listen to the censure of the Lord and of Vaiṣṇavas; / covering his ears, he should leave; if capable, he should administer punishment.
Adopting the manner of the cātaka bird until the fall of the body, O twice-born, / one should abide meditating upon the meaning of the couplet; such is my view.
Just as the cātaka bird, disregarding lakes, oceans, rivers, and the like, / either dies of thirst or begs only from the rain-cloud,
even so should one carefully consider the means; / one's chosen deity is always to be implored: 'May You be my refuge!'
In conformity with one's chosen deity, His devotees, and especially the guru, / one should always remain; one should abandon contrariness.
Having once surrendered, I say, reflecting upon the auspicious nature of both of Them, / one should trust: 'These two will deliver me'—
'From the ocean of worldly existence, O Lords, crowded with friends, sons, and home! / You two alone are my protectors, the destroyers of fear for the surrendered!'
'Whatever I am, and whatever belongs to me in this world and the next, / all that is today offered at Your feet!'
'I am an abode of offenses, one who has abandoned all spiritual means, / and without refuge; therefore, O two Lords, You alone are my refuge!'
'I am yours, O beloved of Rādhikā, in deed, mind, and speech! / O beloved of Kṛṣṇa, I am yours alone! You two alone are my refuge!'
'I have taken refuge in You both, who are mines of masses of compassion! / Bestow Your grace of servitorship upon me, wicked and offending though I am!'

Thus, one wishing to attain her service without delay
should constantly remain reciting this pentad of verses, O best of sages.
These external duties have indeed been described briefly by me; / now the inner, supreme duty of surrendered souls is declared:
Taking refuge carefully in the disposition of a female friend of Kṛṣṇa's beloved, / one should perform service to Them day and night without indolence.
The mantra has been declared, its auxiliary parts, and likewise the qualified persons for it, / and their duties, and likewise the fruit of the mantra for them, O Nārada.
Perform this yourself, and you will attain servitude to Them / upon the exhaustion of your present office, O brāhmaṇa; there is no doubt about this.
To one who has surrendered even once and asks, 'I am yours,' / Hari will grant His personal service; I have no doubt in this matter.
Now I shall describe to you a supreme, wondrous secret, / previously heard by me directly from Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord.
This internal duty has been told to you, O best of sages; / this is the most secret of secrets, and must be concealed with care.
Formerly, chanting the jewel of mantras on the peak of Kailāsa, / meditating upon the divine Nārāyaṇa, I lived in a dense forest.
Then the Lord, being pleased, appeared before me. / When He said, 'Choose a boon,' I opened my eyes,
and saw the Lord situated upon Garuḍa along with His beloved. / Prostrating, I spoke to the husband of Kamalā, the giver of boons:
'That form of Yours, O ocean of mercy, which bestows supreme bliss, / the resting-place of all joy, eternal, embodied, superior to all,'
'which the wise know as Brahman, devoid of material qualities, devoid of action, peaceful— / that I desire to see with my own eyes, O Supreme Lord.'
Then the Lord, the husband of Kamalā, said to me who had surrendered: / 'Today you shall see that form which is desired in your mind.'
'Go to my Vṛndāvana on the western bank of the Yamunā.' / Having said this, the Lord of the universe vanished along with His beloved.
Then I too came to the auspicious bank of the Yamunā, / and there I saw Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of all the lords of the gods,
wearing the attire of a cowherd, charming, endowed with youthful age, / His enchanting left hand resting well upon the shoulder of His beloved,
laughing and making her laugh in the midst of a multitude of cowherd women, / resembling a glistening cloud, the abode of auspicious qualities.
Then Kṛṣṇa, smiling and speaking words like nectar, said to me: / 'I have come within your sight, knowing what you desired, O Rudra.
This extraordinary form of mine which has been seen by you today / is the embodiment of being, consciousness, and bliss, concentrated immaculate love.
Formless, devoid of guṇas, all-pervading, inactive, higher than the highest— / the assemblies of the Upaniṣads speak of this very faultless [form] of mine.
Because it lacks the guṇas born of material nature, and because I am infinite, and thus the Lord, / and because my qualities cannot be fully established, they declare me to be devoid of guṇas.
Because this form of mine cannot be seen by physical eyes, / all these Vedas declare me to be formless, O Maheśvara.
Because I am all-pervading through a portion of consciousness, the wise know me as Brahman; / because I do not act in the phenomenal world, they declare me to be inactive.
Since my partial aspects perform creation and the rest through the qualities of māyā, / I myself do not do anything such as creation, O Śiva.
O Mahādeva, I am overcome by love for these gopīs; / I know no other action, nor even myself, O Nārada.
I sport with her constantly, subdued by her love; / know this Rādhikā, my beloved, to be the supreme deity.
And look all around her: there are hundreds of thousands of companions; / all of them are eternal, O Rudra, just as I have an eternal form.
The cowherds, cows, and cowherd women, and my Vṛndāvana always— / all this is indeed eternal, consisting of the nectar of consciousness and bliss.
Know this Vṛndāvana of mine to be named the Root of Bliss; / merely upon entering it, one would never enter into saṃsāra again.
Having reached my forest, whatever fool goes elsewhere again, / he is indeed a slayer of his own self; true, true is what has been spoken by me.
Abandoning Vṛndāvana, I never go anywhere; / I dwell right here with her at all times.

Thus all that was in your heart has been recounted to you, O Rudra;
tell me now, what else do you wish to hear?
[Śiva said:] 'Then I said to that god, O best of sages: / 'How are you, being such, to be obtained? Tell me that means.''
'Then the Blessed Lord said to me: 'Well said, O Rudra, by you! / This is most secret indeed, and must be concealed with effort.
Whoever, having surrendered to the two of us once, worships [us] having abandoned all other means / in the mood of a gopī, O Lord of gods, he attains me, and no one else.
Or having surrendered once to the two of us, or serves my beloved alone / with undivided sentiment, he attains me without doubt.
He who surrenders to me alone and not to my beloved, O Maheśvara, / he never attains me: thus has it been told to you by me.
Whoever surrenders even once and would even say, "I am yours," / even without any spiritual practice, attains me in this manner without doubt.
Therefore, with every effort, one should go to my beloved for refuge; / having taken shelter of my beloved, O Rudra, you will be able to bring me under your control.
This supreme secret has been proclaimed to you by me; / by you also, O Mahādeva, it must be concealed with effort.
You too, having taken shelter of this Rādhikā, my beloved, / reciting my couple-mantra, dwell always in my abode.''
Śiva said: / Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa, that ocean of compassion, instructed [me] in the supreme mantra in my right ear, performed the purificatory rites,
and vanished with his retinue right there before my eyes, O twice-born. / Since then, I too have remained here continuously.
All this has been proclaimed by me to you, complete with its parts. / Speak now, O foremost of the twice-born: what further do you wish to hear?

5.83.m: Nārada said: / O Lord, all that was asked by me has been told, O guru. / Now I wish to hear the unsurpassed path of emotional love.
Śiva said: / Well asked, O twice-born, you who desire the welfare of all the worlds! / I shall tell you even the secret; hear it as I speak:
The maidservants, male friends, two parents, and beloved women of Hari here / are all eternal, O best of sages, and endowed with virtues.
Just as they are celebrated in the Purāṇas in the manifest pastime, / so they are present in the eternal pastime in the land of Vṛndāvana.
He constantly wanders between the forest and the cow-pens, / herding the cows with his friends, without the slaughter of demons.
His beloved women, considering themselves his own, / delight their beloved through a hidden love alone.
Among them, one should meditate upon oneself as a charming young girl / in the form of a young maiden, endowed with beauty and youth,
skilled in various arts and crafts, suitable for Kṛṣṇa's enjoyment, / yet averse to enjoyment there even when solicited by Kṛṣṇa,
an attendant of Rādhikā, devoted to serving her, / having even greater love for Rādhikā than for Kṛṣṇa,

bringing about their union every day with affection and care,
deeply contented through the emotion of joy born from serving them.

Thinking of oneself in this very manner, one should perform service there,
beginning from the auspicious hour before dawn until the dead of night.
Nārada said: / I wish to hear truly the daily pastime of Hari; / for how can Hari be served with the mind by one who does not know the pastime?
Śiva said: / I do not know that pastime of Hari truly, O Nārada. / Go from here to the goddess Vṛndā; she will tell you the pastime.
She, the attendant of Govinda, surrounded by a multitude of female companions, / stays not far from this place, near the Keśī pilgrimage site.
Sūta said: / Thus spoken to, circumambulating him, delighted, and bowing repeatedly, / Nārada, the best of sages, then went to Vṛndā's hermitage.
Vṛndā too, seeing Nārada, bowed repeatedly and said: / O best of sages, how is it that you have come here?
Nārada said: / I wish to know from you the daily deed of Hari; / tell it to me from the beginning, O fair one, if I am worthy.
Vṛndā said: / I shall tell you even the secret, for you are a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, O Nārada. / You too must not reveal this, which is most secret, greater than the secret.
In the middle of delightful Vṛndāvana, adorned with fifty bowers, / in a bower of wish-fulfilling trees, inside a divine mansion of jewels,
the two lie asleep on a couch, closely embracing one another, / and even though awakened afterwards by birds that do my bidding,
having attained the bliss of a tight embrace and distressed at its interruption, / they do not make up their minds to rise from the couch even slightly.
Then, repeatedly awakened all around by flocks of mynas, parrots, and others / with various words, they rose from their couch.
Seeing the two seated on the couch filled with joy, / the female companions entered and performed the service appropriate for them at that time.
Then, rising from their couch once more at the words of the mynas, / they went each to their own home, agitated by fear and longing.
Awakened in the morning by his mother, Kṛṣṇa quickly arose from his couch, / cleaned his teeth with a twig, and, accompanied by Baladeva,
encouraged by his mother, went to the cowshed surrounded by his friends. / Rādhā too, O twice-born, awakened from her couch by her female companions,
rose, cleaned her teeth, and applied fragrant oils to her body; / having then gone to the bathing platform, she was bathed by her companions.
She went to the dressing chamber, and there her companions adorned her / with various divine ornaments, perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
Then, after entreating her mother-in-law with effort, the female companions / were summoned along with her by Yaśodā to cook their own food.
Nārada said: / Why, O goddess, is she invited by Yaśodā for cooking, / when there are other cooks such as Rohiṇī?
Vṛndā said: / A boon was formerly given to her by Durvāsas, O great sage; / so I heard long ago from the mouth of Kātyāyanī:
"O goddess, whatever food is cooked by you through my grace / will be sweet, rivaling nectar, and will bestow longevity upon the eater."

Thus Yaśodā, fond of her son, always calls upon her:
"May my son be long-lived!" and the virtuous lady [comes] eagerly desiring delicious food.
Delighted on hearing [the call] with approval, she too went to Nanda's residence; / having gone there accompanied by her female companions, she did the cooking.
Kṛṣṇa too, having milked some cows and having had others milked by men, / returned to his house at his father's word, surrounded by his friends.
Having undergone anointing and massage, joyfully bathed by servants, / clad in clean clothes, wearing garlands, his limbs smeared with sandalwood,
gleaming above his neck and forehead with his hair tied in two parts, / adorned with curly locks and a shining forehead-mark shaped like the moon,
his hands shining with bracelets, armlets, amulets, and jeweled rings, / his chest radiant with pearl necklaces, wearing makara-shaped earrings,
called repeatedly by his mother, he entered the dining hall, / holding the hand of a friend and following behind Baladeva.
Then he ate various foods, surrounded by his brother and his friends; / making his friends laugh with various jokes, he laughed himself.
Having thus eaten, rinsed his mouth, and rested for a moment on a divine bed, / sharing and chewing the betel given by his servants,
Kṛṣṇa, wearing the dress of a cowherd, preceded by herds of cows, / was followed along the path with affection by all the residents of Vraja.
Having bowed to his father and mother, and having turned back the assembly [of elders] / and the others appropriately with a glance of his eyes, he went to the forest.
Having entered the forest and played for a moment with his friends, / he then joyfully sported in the forest with various pastimes.
Then, slipping away from everyone, accompanied by two or three dear friends, / he went with joy to the rendezvous, eager to see his beloved.
She too, seeing that Kṛṣṇa had gone to the forest, returned to her home; / under the pretext of worshiping the sun and other deities, and to gather flowers,
having deceived her elders, she went to the forest desiring union with her beloved. / Thus having met in the forest after great effort,
the two joyfully sported throughout the day there with various pastimes; / and seated upon a swing, they were sometimes swung by female friends.
Somewhere, when his flute slipped from his hand and was concealed by his beloved, / Hari, searching for it, was reproached and mocked by the group of beloved maidens;
provoked to laughter in many ways by their laughter, he stayed there; / elsewhere, [they wandered] joyfully in a grove of the forest served by the spring breeze.
Entering [the water], sprinkling each other with sandal-water and saffron-water / released from syringe devices, they smeared one another with those fragrant pastes.
The female companions also sprinkled them thus, and those two sprinkled them in return, / in the groves of the forest enjoyed everywhere by the spring breezes.
Engaged in various pastimes appropriate to each time, together with their attendants, O twice-born one, / weary, having approached the foot of a tree somewhere, O best of sages,
sitting down on a divine seat, they drank sweet wine. / Then, intoxicated by the passion of the wine, their eyes closed with sleepiness,
holding each other's hand, fallen under the power of Kama's arrows, / longing for love-play, their speech and mind faltering on the path, they entered a bower.
And then they sported there like a cow-elephant and the leader of the herd. / The female companions too, intoxicated by the wines and their eyes afflicted with drowsiness,
all lay down all around in the lovely bowers. / With a separate body for each, Kṛṣṇa also, the all-pervading lord,
went into the presence of them all simultaneously, urged repeatedly by his beloved; / having given pleasure to all of them, like the king of elephants to female elephants,
he went to the lake together with his beloved and those women for the sake of play. / Then the two, with their attendants, sported there sprinkling each other with water.
Adorned with garments, garlands, and divine sandal-paste, and with ornaments, / right there on the bank of the lake, in a house made of divine jewels,
fruits and roots had already been prepared by me, O sage. / Hari, having eaten first, surrounded by his beloved,
attended by two or three women, went to a bed made of flowers. / There, being served with betel, fans, foot-massaging, and other attentions,
laughing, he rejoiced with them, remembering his beloved. / When Hari had fallen asleep, Rādhikā also, accompanied by her attendants, joyful at heart,
with her very life-breath resting in him, ate his food remnants; / and having eaten just a little, she went to the chamber with the bed,
to gaze upon her beloved's lotus-face, like a female cakora bird upon the moon. / Chewed betel offered by the maidens stationed there,
as well as [fresh] betel nuts, she ate, distributing them among her dear companions. / Kṛṣṇa also, wishing to overhear their unrestrained conversation among themselves,
appeared as though asleep, though awake, covered by a cloth. / And they, making sport of looking for some reason from an inference,
biting their tongues with their teeth and looking at one another's face, / as if dissolved in an ocean of shame, said nothing for a moment.
Then, immediately removing the cloth from his limb, / laughing and making him laugh, they said: 'You have feigned sleep very well!'
Thus sporting with diverse jests together with their attendants, / and having enjoyed the pleasure of sleep for a moment, O best of sages,
sitting joyfully with their attendants on a wide, divine seat, / wagering necklaces, kisses, embraces, and ornaments against each other,
they played with dice in love, accompanied by witty conversation. / Even when defeated by his beloved, saying, 'Indeed, I am the winner!'
he set out to seize her necklace and other ornaments, and was struck by her. / Thus struck by her with her hand on his lotus-face,
Kṛṣṇa became despondent in mind and resolved to leave, [saying]: / 'If I have been defeated by you, O lady, take what was wagered;
a kiss and the like have been granted by me!' Having said this, she acted thus, / in order to see the curve of his eyebrows and hear his words of scolding.
Then, hearing the war of words between the mainas and the parrots, / both desiring to go home, departed from that place.
Kṛṣṇa, having bid farewell to his beloved, went toward the cows, / while she, accompanied by her circle of female friends, went to the temple of the Sun.
Hari, having gone a certain distance, then turned back, / assumed the guise of a brahmin, and went toward the temple of the Sun.
Requested there by her female companions, he worshipped the Sun / with Vedic verses improvised right then, permeated with humor.
Then those clever women, recognizing their beloved who had been indicated, / plunged into an ocean of bliss and knew neither themselves nor anything else.
Having spent two and a half yāmas in this manner through various pastimes, O sage, / the women went home, and Kṛṣṇa went to the cows.
Having joined his companions, Kṛṣṇa gathered the cows from all sides; / he came to Vraja with joy, sounding his flute, O sage.
Then Nanda and all the others, hearing the sound of Hari's flute, / and seeing the dome of the sky covered with a veil of cow-dust,
leaving aside all work, women, children, and all others as well, / went to meet Kṛṣṇa, eager to behold him.
On the royal road, at the gate of Vraja, where all the inhabitants of Vraja were, / Kṛṣṇa too, having approached them, in due order and according to propriety,
[honored them] through looks, touches, words, and glances preceded by smiles, / and the elder cowherds with physical and verbal salutations,
and his two parents and Rohiṇī with full-length prostrations, O Nārada, / and likewise his beloved through modesty indicated only with the corner of his eye.
Thus worshiped as appropriate by the inhabitants of Vraja, / and having led the cows into the cow-pen on all sides,
he went to his own home together with his brother, requested by his parents. / Having bathed, drunk [water], and eaten a little there, encouraged by his mother,
he went again to the cow-pen, desiring to milk the milk of the cows; / and having milked some, having caused others to be milked, and having made some drink,
he went home with his father, obeying hundreds of loving impulses. / There, with his father, paternal uncles, their sons, and with Bala,
he ate various kinds of foods—chewables, suckables, and the like. / Attentive to him, even before he asked, Rādhikā right then
sent cooked foods to his home through a female friend. / And Hari, praising them, ate them together with his father and the rest,
and went to the assembly hall filled with bards and other attendants. / The female companions who had earlier arrived there carrying cooked dishes,
having received many dishes in return given by Yaśodā, / took the remnants of Kṛṣṇa's meal given by her there.
Everything was brought by them and offered to Rādhikā; / and she also, joined by her group of female friends, ate it in due order.
Adorned by her friends, she stood ready to go to the rendezvous. / Then a certain female friend was sent by me from right here;
led to the rendezvous by her near the Yamunā, / in this bower of wish-fulfilling trees, in this house made of divine jewels,
in attire suited for a bright or dark night, she arrived surrounded by her friends. / Kṛṣṇa too, having seen various entertaining sights there,
and having heard charming songs for Kātyāyanī, / and having pleased those [singers] properly with wealth, grain, and the like,
honored by the people and fed by his mother, went to a friend's house; / and when his mother had departed, from that house,
he went unnoticed to the rendezvous where his beloved was. / Meeting there, the two of them sported among the groves of the forest,
with various pastimes accompanied by the rāsa-dance, dramatic dance, and laughter. / Having spent two and a half yāmas of the night in sport in this way,
desiring to sleep, unnoticed by the female birds, they entered a bower; / in solitude, on a delightful pleasure-bed fashioned with flowers,
the two of them lay asleep, attended by their own female companions. / Thus has the complete daily routine of Hari been narrated to you.

Even sinners are liberated by hearing this, O Nārada.
Nārada said: I am blessed, I have been favored by you, O goddess, beyond doubt,

since the daily pastime of Hari has been revealed to me today.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus and circumambulated her, and also honored by her,

Nārada, the best of sages, disappeared, O Brahmin.
By me too this has all been recounted in proper order.

One should always recite with effort the unsurpassed pair of mantras.
Formerly this was obtained with exertion by Rudra from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa;

it was spoken by him to Nārada, and told to me by Nārada.
Having performed the initiatory rites, this has likewise been told to you by me.

By you also this most wondrous secret must be kept concealed.
Śaunaka said: I have attained my purpose, becoming [fulfilled] through your favor, O guru,

since the secret of secrets has been revealed by you to me.
Sūta said: Observing these duties, murmuring the mantra day and night,

before long you will attain servitude to him, beyond doubt.
I too am going, O Brahmin, to the eternal abode of the Lord,
of the guru of the guru, on the bank of the daughter of the sun, and of Gopīśvara.

This supreme, sacred, magnificent account was spoken by Maheśa;
those people who hear it endowed with devotion go to the eternal abode of Acyuta.

It is auspicious, brings fame, grants long life, health, and desired success;
it is the cause of heaven, liberation, and prosperity, and destroys sins.

The men devoted to Viṣṇu who recite it daily with devotion
never return from the world of Viṣṇu under any circumstances.

5.84.m:
The sages said:
O Sūta, O Sūta of great fortune, delight of Romaharṣaṇa!
A delightful story has been spoken by you, giving joy to the world.

The greatly wondrous deeds of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, O greatly fortunate one,
have all been heard as spoken by you, and peace of mind has arisen from that.

Ah, the glorification of Śrī Kṛṣṇa grants the ultimate goal to devotees!
From that, O greatly fortunate one, who would not obtain peace of mind?

Therefore, we wish to hear again the great deeds of the glorious Kṛṣṇa,
and also other things: vows, gifts, worship, and the like,

and ritual bathing, O greatly fortunate one, how and by whom it was performed formerly;
tell all that in detail, so that we may obtain peace of mind.

Sūta said: Well asked, O best of the twice-born, supreme deliverance for the worlds!
You have attained your purpose, your minds filled with devotion to Kṛṣṇa.

The holy deeds of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which grant supreme joy to the virtuous,
I shall proclaim, O best of the twice-born, a great and excellent narrative.

Once Nārada, beloved of the Lord, wandering through the worlds,
saw Ambarīṣa in Mathurā, intent upon the worship of Kṛṣṇa,

greatly fortunate, dedicated to vows, the best of sages saw [him].
Having honored the eminent sage who had arrived, that best of sages,

his mind delighted with faith, questioned you indeed:
Ambarīṣa said: What is called the supreme Brahman by those who expound the Veda, O sage,

that is the lotus-eyed god, the supreme Nārāyaṇa himself,
who is formless, possessing form, the ruler, manifest and unmanifest, eternal,

consisting of all beings, unthinkable—how is that Hari to be meditated upon,
in whom this entire universe is woven lengthwise and crosswise, and established,

unmanifest, single, supreme, renowned as the Paramātman,
from whom is the origin and the rest of the universe, who, having fashioned Brahmā,

gave to him the Vedas established within himself?
How is he to be worshipped, he who grants all the aims of human life,

difficult to approach even for yogins? Speak of that with compassion!
Those who have not worshipped Govinda do not know the arising of their welfare,

nor do they obtain the excellent fruit of austerities, sacrifices, and gifts.
And whoever has not tasted the nectar of Govinda's lotus feet

cannot conceive of the abundant fruit that lies beyond the path of desire.
Except for the worship of Hari, which averts the flood of misfortunes,

I see no other supreme expiation for living beings, O sage,
on the dance of whose brow all perfections are said to attend.

How is he to be worshipped, that Keśava who destroys afflictions?
How is that Lord Nārāyaṇa to be served by men?

Being pleased, tell all this to me for the welfare of the world!
That Lord is fond of devotion; by what devotion is he pleased?

How may devotion toward him arise? How is he worshipped by all?
You are a Vaiṣṇava, dear to that Hari, and a knower of the highest truth.

Therefore, I ask you alone, O Brahmin, best among knowers of Brahman!
A question about Hari purifies the listener, or the speaker, or the inquirer,

just as the water of Kṛṣṇa's feet [purifies].
Difficult to obtain is the human body for embodied souls, fragile in a moment;

even there, I consider the sight of one dear to Vaikuṇṭha to be rare.
In this transmigratory existence, even half a moment's company with the virtuous is a treasure for men,

from which all four aims of human life are attained.
Lord, your journey is for the well-being of all embodied beings,

just as the way of parents of renowned fame is for children.
The conduct of gods brings both sorrow and joy to living beings,

but that of the virtuous whose souls are devoted to Acyuta, such as you, brings only joy.
As men worship the gods, so indeed the gods treat them,

like a shadow, assisting actions; but the virtuous are compassionate to the wretched.
Therefore, Lord, instruct me in the Vaiṣṇava duty,

by the teaching of which one obtains the fruit born of the Vedas.
Nārada said: Well asked, O king, by you who possess devotion to Viṣṇu,

who know the supreme duty, the sole service of Mādhava,
when Viṣṇu is worshipped, the universe becomes worshipped;

when Hari, who comprises all deities, is pleased, the moving and unmoving world is pleased.
By the mere remembrance of whom the collection of great sins

comes to destruction in that very instant, that Hari alone is to be served.
What man endowed with senses, O king, when death is on every side,

would not worship the lotus foot of Mukunda, which is worshipped by sages and gods?
Heard, recited, meditated upon, respected, and rejoiced in,

the true duty instantly purifies even a hero who harms the world.
He who is this cause, effect, and the rest, and the cause even of the cause,

having no other cause, the yogin, the soul of the world, consisting of the world,
minute, vast, subtle, gross, devoid of qualities, bearing qualities, great,

unborn, beyond birth and dissolution—that Hari is always to be meditated upon.
This has been properly resolved by you, O bull among men,

that you ask about the Bhāgavata duties which sustain the universe.
In the association of the virtuous, the pure narratives of Kṛṣṇa,

who is worthy of praise, become an elixir for the mind and the ear.
For this god is attained through devotional feeling; you yourself know that.

Nevertheless, I shall speak for the welfare of the world, out of respect for you.
That which they call the supreme Brahman, higher than primal nature and the spirit,

by whose māyā all is pervaded, that Acyuta gives everything:
sons, a wife, long life, kingship, heaven, and liberation.

Worshipped with devotion, the unconquered one gives all that is desired.
Those human beings who are devoted to him in action, mind, and speech,
I shall declare their vows for His pleasure, O best of kings: / non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and lack of cunning;
these are said to be mental vows for the satisfaction of Hari. / Eating once a day, eating only at night, fasting, and living on unsolicited food—

Thus has the bodily observance of men been spoken, O ruler of men:
study of the Veda, glorification of Viṣṇu, and speaking the truth.
and absence of slander: this, O king, is the highest vocal vow. / One should always and everywhere chant the names of the wielder of the discus.
There is no impurity in chanting His name, since He makes all things pure. / By a man adhering to the conduct of caste and stage of life, the Supreme Person,
Viṣṇu, is worshipped; there is no other path that causes His satisfaction. / And by women devoted to the pleasure and welfare of their husbands, with restraint of mind, speech, and body,
and with vows, Vāsudeva, the ocean of compassion, is worshipped. / Worship of Kṛṣṇacandra, who assumes the form of the best of the twice-born,
should also be performed by women and Śūdras through the path taught in the Āgamas. / The three castes are devoted to worshipping according to the path taught in the Vedas,
while women, Śūdras, and others should be devoted to worshipping by means of the Name. / Neither by rituals of worship, nor by sacrifices, nor by vows is Mādhava
pleased; He is declared to love devotion alone. / For women devoted to their husbands, the husband alone is indeed the deity.
He indeed is to be worshipped with devotion to Viṣṇu, through actions of mind, speech, and body. / Viṣṇu's [worship] must be performed with faith, meditating on the husband in the heart.
And for Śūdras, the worship of the deity is performed through the Name. / All should act through the path of the Āgamas that conforms to the Vedas.
Women also have the right to the worship and other rites of Viṣṇu / if they are devoted to pleasing their husbands; this is the eternal Vedic revelation.
Whatever vow is prescribed for anyone according to the duty suitable to their lineage, / if one performs that very vow, Keśava is pleased with them.
With oblations in the fire, with flowers in water, with meditation in the heart, / and with recitation in the solar orb, the wise continually worship Hari.
Non-violence is the first flower; restraint of the senses is the second; / compassion for all beings is the third, and forbearance is the fourth;
tranquility is the fifth flower, and self-control the sixth; the seventh / is meditation, and truth is the eighth; with these Keśava is pleased.
With these eight flowers alone is Hari truly pleased when worshipped. / There are indeed other external flowers, O best of men,
offered with devotion, by which Viṣṇu is well pleased when worshipped: / water is the flower of Varuṇa; ghee, milk, and curd belong to Soma;
food and the like belong to Prajāpati; incense and lamps belong to Agni; / and fruits, flowers, and such are the fifth, belonging to Vanaspati;
kuśa-grass, roots, and the like belong to the Earth; perfume and sandalwood belong to Vāyu; / faith is called the flower of Viṣṇu, and musical instruments are known as the realm of Viṣṇu.
When worshipped with these flowers, Viṣṇu also becomes gracious. / The sun, fire, a Brahmin, cows, a Vaiṣṇava, the sky, the wind, water,
the earth, the self, and all living beings are the places of worship for Hari. / In the sun one should worship through the recitation of mantras, then in fire through oblations,
in the foremost of Brahmins through hospitality, in cows through mouthfuls of food and liquids, / in a Vaiṣṇava by honoring him as a relative, in the heart through devotion to meditation,

in the wind with the thought of the vital breath, in water with offerings preceded by water, / on a bare patch of ground through the core of mantras, with enjoyable offerings, the Self within oneself;
one should worship the all-pervading Lord as the knower of the field in all beings with equanimity. / In these seats, meditating with a concentrated mind on His form,
endowed with four arms, holding a conch, discus, mace, and lotus, peaceful, one should worship Him. / When Brahmins are worshipped, He is indeed worshipped; there is no doubt.
And when they are reproached, O king, the all-pervading Lord is reproached. / The foundation upon which the Veda and the legal treatise proceed—
those Brahmins are regarded as the purifying, supreme form of Viṣṇu.

All good in the world is attained through dharma alone; the course of dharma is from the Veda and the legal treatises, O king. / Truly, the course of both of these on earth is the Brahmins; when they are worshipped here, the Lord of the universe is worshipped.
Neither by sacrifices and yogas, nor by other austerities, nor by the practice of yoga, nor by elaborate worship / is the all-pervading God of gods pleased, as He is by pleasing the earthly gods.
He is friendly to Brahmins, the knower of Brahman, Brahmā, and the promoter of the Vedic Brahman; / only through Brahmins is that deity of Brahman pleased when they are satisfied.
Even if the ancestors of both maternal and paternal lineages have been plunged long in hell, / they go to heaven at that very moment when a son worships Hari.
What is the use of their life here, what is the use of their action resembling beasts, / whose minds are not inclined toward Vāsudeva, who comprises the universe?
I shall declare His meditation, which has not been seen by anyone; / listen, O king, to absolute isolation, pure and free from defilement.
Just as a lamp standing in a windless place, motionless and free from breeze, / blazes forth and dispels all darkness, O wise one,
even so the self, freed from faults, becomes truly healthy, / desireless, motionless, heroic, having neither friend nor foe;
grief and joy, and dejection, greed, envy, delusion, / agitation, chatter, and bewilderment, and pleasures and pains are shed;
and it is released from all sensory objects of the senses; / then, possessing pure knowledge, it attains the state of absolute isolation.
Through the process of its flame, the lamp dries up the oil, / supported by the wick, O king of kings, free from duality and free from wind;
then it emits soot from the oil, O wise one, / and a black streak is seen at the tip of the lamp, O wise one;
drawing in that oil by itself, it becomes pure through its light. / Standing within the body, likewise, it dries up the oil of karma;
turning sensory objects into soot, it makes them visible, / and becoming spotless like a flame, it shines forth entirely by itself.
Free from the winds known as anger, greed, and the like, / becoming desireless and motionless, its splendor shines forth on its own.
It sees the entire three worlds abiding in their proper places by its own light. / This form of pure knowledge has thus been described to you.
And I will declare the two kinds of meditation on the wielder of the discus: / through the form of pure knowledge He is seen with the supreme eye.
The great-souled ones yoked in yoga, intent upon the highest reality, / see Him whom the bewildered do not see, the all-knowing and all-beholding.
Without hands and feet, He moves everywhere; / He grasps all the three worlds, both immovable and movable.
Without nose and mouth, He smells and eats, O king; / earless, He hears all; He is the witness of all, the Lord of the universe.
Formless, yet connected with forms, controlling the five classes of senses, / He who is the life-breath of the entire world is worshipped by movable and immovable beings.
Tongueless, He speaks everything in accordance with the Vedas and scriptures; / skinless, He experiences the touch of all things.
He is eternal bliss, of solitary perception, uniform, without support, / devoid of qualities, free from possessiveness, all-pervading, endowed with qualities, spotless, and sinless;
unmastered, yet the master of all, all-giving, the best of knowers of all; / He has no mother, and He is indeed the all-pervading Lord composed of all.
And whoever, with single-minded intellect, beholds this meditation consisting of all, / goes to the supreme abode, formless and like nectar.
Now I shall tell you the second [form of meditation]; listen to that, O highly intelligent one: / [it is] embodied in form, possessing attributes, yet formless and free from illness.
Because the entire, peerless universe is pervaded by his dwelling, / therefore he is called Vāsudeva, O delight of kings.
His brilliance resembles that of a raining cloud; / he possesses four arms, shining like the splendour of the sun, the lord of the gods.
In his right hand shines the conch decorated with gold and gems; / his Kaumodakī mace destroys great demons;
And in the left hand of that great soul, O hero, it shines; / a great lotus rich in sweet fragrance is held in his right hand,
Ever shining, armed with weapons, possessing the splendour of a lotus, / having a neck like a conch, a well-rounded face, and eyes resembling lotus petals,
Hṛṣīkeśa, radiant with teeth resembling kunda blossoms; / the lower lip of Guḍākeśa has the form of coral;
The lotus-eyed one shines also with a radiant diadem; / and Keśava [is splendid] with his vast form and broad chest,
Janārdana shining, marked with the Kaustubha gem; / and he gleams with two earrings radiant as the sun's splendour;
Hari ever shines with the sacred mark of Śrīvatsa, / with armlets, bracelets, and pearl necklaces resembling constellations;
Radiant in body, victorious, best among conquerors, / that Govinda also shines with golden-coloured garments;
Hari shines on his fingers equipped with signet rings, / fully adorned with all weapons and celestial ornaments,
Mounted upon the son of Vinatā, creator of the worlds, lord of the universe. / The person who thus meditates [upon him] constantly with single-minded focus,
Is freed from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. / All this division of meditation on the lord of the universe has been told to you.

5.85.m: Ambarīṣa said: / Well done, well done, O best of sages, granter of grace to the world! / You have explained the meditation on Viṣṇu, both with attributes and without attributes.
Now, O noble doer of compassion, speak the characteristic of devotion— / of what kind it is performed, by whom, in what manner, where, and when.
Sūta said: / Hearing what was spoken by the best of kings, the sage, delighted, replied to the monarch: / 'Listen, O king, I shall declare to you fully the devotion to Hari that takes away all sins.'
'Now I shall describe the manifold devotion that destroys sin; / manifold devotion is declared as originating from the mind, speech, and body.
It can be worldly, Vedic, and likewise spiritual. / That remembering of the Vedas through intellect by means of meditation and retention,
Which brings joy to Viṣṇu, is called mental devotion. / By utterings of mantras and the Veda, by unceasing reflections,
And by recitations and forest texts, vocal devotion is spoken of. / By vows, fasts, observances, and conquest of the five senses,
Bodily devotion, fulfilling all aims, is designated. / By ornaments marked with gold and jewels, and with diverse words,
With garments, amulets, threads, burning fans held aloft, / with dance, instruments, songs, and offerings of every presentation,
And the worship performed by men with foods to chew and eat, grains and drinks / directed toward Nārāyaṇa—that is regarded as worldly devotion.
That bodily devotion is designated as accomplishing all ends. / Recitations of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and studies of the Saṃhitās,
Which are performed for Viṣṇu—that devotion is called Vedic. / The action performed through Vedic mantras, oblations, and sacrifices is considered Vedic:
The agnihotra to be performed on the new moon and full moon days, / the consumption of oblations, giving of dakṣiṇā, ritual cakes, preparation of caru,
The iṣṭi sacrifice, dhṛti rites, drinking of Soma, and sacrificial rites of every kind; / fire, earth, wind, space, light, Śaṅkara, the sun—
Action performed dedicated to him has Viṣṇu as its deity in every way. / Spiritual devotion, abiding in Brahman, is twofold, O king.
Hear, O monarch, of that known as Sāṃkhya and that arisen from yoga, as stated: / the principles, beginning with pradhāna, are twenty-four in number,
Inanimate, to be experienced, while the puruṣa is the twenty-fifth; / he is declared conscious, the agent and the enjoyer of actions,
The self, eternal, imperishable, the overseer, the impeller; / the puruṣa is unmanifest and eternal, and the cause, the great lord.
The creation of principles, the creation of inner states, and the creation of elements in truth; / by counting and enumeration, pradhāna consists of the guṇas.
Having known similarity and difference, and pradhāna as different in nature, / and this cause of Brahman is called desire.
The fact of pradhāna being impelled is called its difference; / agency belongs to Brahman everywhere, and puruṣa has non-agency;
This is called equality with inanimate pradhāna. / The distinction among principles, cause and effect,
The purpose and the impulsion, having known by complete enumeration of principles, / is declared as counted by the wise who reflect upon victory.

Having thus understood its true nature, reality, and enumeration in truth,
the wise know that the reality of the elements is even greater than the reality of brahman.
This devotion performed by followers of Sāṃkhya is remembered as spiritual devotion. / Listen, O monarch, I shall also tell you of devotion born of yoga.
Ever intent on breath control, meditative, with senses controlled, / observant of the vow of eating begged food, with all senses withdrawn,
Fixing the mind in the heart, meditating upon the great lord / seated on the pericarp of the heart lotus, wearing yellow garments, having beautiful eyes,
Seeing his radiant face, his sacred thread and hips, / white-coloured, four-armed, hands bestowing boons and freedom from fear—
This mental perfection born of yoga is remembered as supreme devotion to Viṣṇu. / He who is thus devoted to God is said to possess devotion to Viṣṇu.
Thus manifold devotion has been set forth, O delight of kings; / according to their divisions, these are sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa,
To be known as of various kinds, directed toward Viṣṇu of boundless splendour. / Just as a fire with blazing flames reduces kindling to ash,
Even so does devotion to the Lord burn away sins instantly.

As long as a person on earth does not hear devotion to Viṣṇu—the nectar-essence directly present, the sole quintessence of all tastes— / so long does he suffer the pains born of many bodies from the assaults of hundreds of births, old age, and death.
The infinite Lord, when praised, when his fame is contemplated within, when his majesty is heard, / destroys all sin completely, as the wind destroys a cloud, or the sun darkness.
The inner self does not obtain such purity by gifts, worship of the gods, bathing in holy waters, study, righteous conduct, or penances, / as it does when the infinite Lord resides in the heart.

Those stories alone are truly pure, O lord of men, those alone are salutary, true to the Lord Hari, / where the holy form is celebrated, and where the fame of the righteous, heard [by all], is listened to.

You are blessed, steadfast king, bearer of the burden of dharma, whose heart is intent solely on meditating upon Puruṣottama, / since this steadfast disposition of yours, endowed with auspicious fortune and merit toward Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, is engaged in listening.
Without worshipping Hari with devotion, Viṣṇu the boon-giver, the imperishable, / how could the highest good come to pass, O king, for a man who is proud of himself?
Free of māyā, the origin of māyā, he is won over by devotion that is free from deceit, O king; / he is a righteous person, and you know that yourself.

The pure essence of dharma is not unknown to you, O king; yet, out of reverence for the Vaiṣṇava tradition, / you ask me again about the supreme abode in the course of recounting, desiring the nectar of the narrative.

Beyond this, I see no mutual merit suited to nurture supreme satisfaction, / since the good eagerly enjoy the boundless virtues of the Infinite One, the treasuries of endless welfare, enjoying an abundance of feeling.
Brāhmaṇas, the wish-granting cow, truth, faith, sacrifices and austerities, / revelation, tradition, compassion, initiation, and peaceful states are the bodies of Hari.
The sun, the moon, the wind, the earth, the waters, the sky, the directions, / Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—the all-pervading Lord consists of all beings.
Endowed with universal form, he himself made this moving and unmoving world; / entering a brāhmaṇa himself, he ever consumes the food [offered].

Therefore, worship the brāhmaṇas, the dust of whose feet is the abode of holy places, who are the earthly realm of the Supreme Self, / who are the all-in-all of the fortune of merit, and who are identical with the universal Self.
He who sees a wise and virtuous brāhmaṇa with the mindset that he is Viṣṇu, / and who is devoted solely to his own prescribed duties—he alone is a Vaiṣṇava.
This secret has been briefly spoken by me, for it is my time / to go and bathe in the Gaṅgā; there is no further opportunity for conversation.
This month of Mādhava has arrived, holy and dear to Mādhava; / in it too, the bright seventh day is extremely rare at the Gaṅgā.
On the bright seventh of Vaiśākha, the Jāhnavī was formerly swallowed in anger by Jahnu, / and then released again from his right ear.
Whoever, having bathed properly according to the rule, worships the goddess Gaṅgā, the girdle of the sky, / on that day—that man is blessed and full of merit.
The mortal who propitiates the gods and the ancestors according to the rule on that day, / the Gaṅgā perceives him directly as one who has completed his bath, with sins vanished.
There is no month equal to Mādhava, no river equal to the Gaṅgā; / this conjunction is indeed rare, and is attained only by devotion to Hari.
Arising from the water of Viṣṇu's feet, arrived from the world of Brahmā, / she purifies the three worlds tirelessly with her three streams.
She is the ladder for ascending to heaven, constantly granting joy, / removing the eruptions of many evils, saving from distress.
Residing in the matted hair of glorious Maheśa, destroying sorrow, / she dispels the pleasing dalliance of desire in the minds of those who worship her.
Granting liberation to the lineage of Sagara, upholding dharma, / moving along the three paths, the goddess adorns the worlds.
Through seeing, touching, bathing, chanting, meditating, and serving, / she purifies men, both meritorious and unmeritorious, by the thousands.
Those by whom 'Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā' is uttered at the three junctures of the day, / even while dwelling far away, it destroys their sins accumulated over three births.
A man who remembers the Gaṅgā even from thousands of leagues away, / even if he has done evil deeds, attains the supreme destination.
On the bright seventh of Vaiśākha, she is especially rare; / she is attained, O protector of the earth, through the grace of Hari and the brāhmaṇas.
There is no month equal to Mādhava, no lord equal to Mādhava, / who is the refuge of a person sinking in the ocean of sins.
Whatever is given, muttered, offered into fire, or bathed in with devotion in the month of Mādhava, / that merit becomes inexhaustible, O king, exceeding hundreds of millions.
Just as Hari, Nārāyaṇa, the Soul of all, is foremost among the gods, / and just as the Gāyatrī is among chants, so is the Jāhnavī among rivers.
Just as Umā is among all women, the sun among radiant lights, / the gaining of good health among acquisitions, and the brāhmaṇa among two-legged beings,
just as benevolence is among merits, the Veda among sciences, / the syllable Om among mantras, and reflection on the Self among meditations,
just as truth and abiding in one's own duty are best among austerities, / purity of wealth among purities, and fearlessness among gifts,
and just as the destruction of greed is considered the chief virtue among virtues, / so is that Mādhava regarded as the best month among months.
Whatever ancestral rite, sacrifice, gift, fasting, / austerity, study, worship, and the like is performed then, is declared to bear inexhaustible fruit.
Sins end with Vaiśākha, darkness ends with the sun, / and merits end with malicious slander and doing harm to others.
Whatever little bathing, giving, and the like is done in the month of Kārtika / when the sun is in Libra, O king, becomes multiplied by a parārdha.
It is a thousand times greater than that in Māgha when the sun is in Capricorn, / and a hundred times more than that in Vaiśākha when the sun is in Aries.
Blessed and meritorious are those men in the month of Vaiśākha / who, having bathed in the morning according to rule, worship the foe of Madhu.
Morning bathing in Vaiśākha, sacrifice, gifts, fasting, / sacrificial food, and celibacy destroy grave sins.
Yet in the Kali age, O king, this will become hidden, / along with the horse sacrifice and so on, for such is the glorification of Mādhava.
The holy horse sacrifice does not take place in Kali at all; / this rite of the month of Mādhava is equal to a horse sacrifice.
The merit of a horse sacrifice, which grants the fruits of heaven and liberation, / will not be known in Kali by sinful men whose minds are prone to evil.
In that [age], men who are sinful by nature must go to the ocean of hell; / therefore its propagation was made rare by him.

5.86.m: Sūta said: / Having heard these words of the great-souled Nārada, / the royal sage Ambarīṣa, filled with wonder, spoke these words:
Ambarīṣa said: / Setting aside the holy months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, O great sage, / why do you praise the month of Vaiśākha as superior to all months?
Why is Mādhava, dear to Mādhava, greater than all? / What is the rule there, what gift, what austerity, and who is the deity?
To me, who have been purified by the dust of your lotus feet, O sage, / you ought to grant favor by the grace of your instruction.
You know dharma, you are the uplifter of the paths of dharma, O great sage; / you alone know the meaning of all truths and are the teacher of dharma.
The doer, the instructor, the consenter, the approver, and the promoter— / these are remembered by knowers of the treatises, O best of sages, as sharing an equal portion.
Whatever fruit is attained through vows, sacrificial sessions, austerities, and gifts, / all of that is obtained merely through the teaching of dharma.
Whatever bath in a sacred ford, austerity, or sacrificial rite one performs, O sage, / he who initiates it also becomes a sharer in its fruit.
Whatever the superior person practices, that very thing other people do; / whatever standard he sets, the world follows.
Therefore you ought to teach that wonderful dharma; / awakening by a guru, and the proper combinations of place and time, are hard to obtain.
No circumstances—even the acquisition of a kingdom and the like— / cool our heart in the way your arrival does.
Sūta said: / Then Nārada, the best of sages, following the radiance of his teeth gleaming in a gentle, soft smile, / replied to Ambarīṣa:
Nārada said: / Listen, O King, for your benefit and the benefit of the world, I shall declare / the rite of the month of Mādhava, which was previously heard from Brahmā.
Birth in Bhāratavarṣa is difficult to obtain, and still rarer is humanity; / when human life has been obtained in the world, rarer still is engaging in one's own dharma.
Even rarer than that, O King, is devotion to Vāsudeva; / and there too, difficult to obtain is the month of Mādhava, beloved of Mādhava.
Those men who, having attained that month, / perform bathing, gift-giving, silent recitation, and other rites according to rule, are blessed and accomplished.
By merely seeing them, even sinners are cleansed of guilt; / imbued with love for the Lord, they become seekers of dharma.
Those who have bathed in the morning in the month of Mādhava, accompanied by observances, / sport in the Nandana grove for ten million years.
Just as there is no body of water in the world equal to the ocean, / even so there is no month like Vaiśākha, which is dear to Mādhava.
Sins remain in the bodies of mortals only so long / as the month of Mādhava, the destroyer of impurities, does not arrive.
Even the last five days of that month, / beginning from the eleventh, are indeed equal to the entire month.
