Those by whom the god Mādhava, the slayer of Madhu, has been worshipped in Vaiśākha / with various offerings, O king of kings, have attained the fruit of their birth.
What, indeed, of the rarest things is not obtained in the month of Mādhava / by bathing and by worshipping the Supreme Lord according to rule?
Nothing has been given, no oblation offered, no mantra chanted, no death undergone at a sacred ford / by those who have never meditated on Nārāyaṇa, the remover of all sins.
The birth of those men in this world is to be known as fruitless, O King. / The man who is a miser when wealth is present,
and who dies without giving, his wealth is indeed useless. / Birth in a good family is obtained through austerities such as bathing at sacred fords;
yet without gift-giving, O King, nothing at all stays with a person. / From the glorification of bathing in Vaiśākha, even for a duration of five days,
birth in a noble lineage is attained, as well as manifold splendors: / a good son, an illustrious family, O King, wealth, grain, excellent wives,
an auspicious birth, a peaceful death, abundant enjoyments, and happiness itself, / ever greater delight in giving, generosity, and supreme fortitude.
By the grace of that god Viṣṇu, the great soul, / Nārāyaṇa, the desired attainments come into being, O King.
In the month of Ūrja, in the month of Tapas, and in Mādhava, beloved of Mādhava, / having bathed, and with devotion having especially worshipped Dāmodara, Mādhava, the slayer of Madhu,
and given gifts according to one's capacity, / a man attains earthly happiness and then goes to Hari's abode.
The succession of sins acquired across many births dissolves through bathing in Mādhava, / just as darkness does at sunrise, O King; Brahmā himself declared this teaching to me.
Viṣṇu spread wide the observance of the month known as Mādhava; / having reflected on Yama's secret words, he brought it to the mortal world.
Therefore, when this month of Mādhava has arrived, Vaiṣṇavas, / having bathed in sacred water at a ford of the Gaṅgā that purifies mortals,
or at the Revā, O great King, or at the Yamunā or Śāradā, / in the morning before the sun has risen, according to rule, O best of kings,
and having worshipped the Lord of gods, Mukunda, the slayer of Madhu, / [and having obtained] the good fortune of sons, grandsons, and wealth, as well as desired pleasures,
having enjoyed [these], at the end of their austerities they attain imperishable heaven. / Knowing this, O fortunate one, worship the slayer of Madhu.
Having bathed according to proper rule, particularly in Vaiśākha, / and having venerated the god Govinda, the stainless Nārāyaṇa,
you will obtain happiness, a son, riches, and the abode of Hari. / Having bowed to the God of gods, Mādhava, the destroyer of sins,
one should undertake this vow on the full-moon day of Madhu, O King, / equipped with restraints and observances, and having given something according to one's means,
eating sacrificial food, sleeping on the ground, established in the vow of celibacy, / emaciated by penances such as the kṛcchra, meditating on Nārāyaṇa in the heart.
Then, having reached the full moon of Vaiśākha, one should offer honey, sesame seeds, and the like, / food to the foremost brahmins, and with devotion a cow along with a priestly gift.
And one should request the earthly gods that that bath be without fault. / Just as Lakṣmī is dear to Mādhava, the Lord of the world, O King,
in that very way the month of Mādhava is beloved of the slayer of Madhu. / A mortal endowed with these rules who has thus bathed for twelve years
should perform the concluding rite according to ability for the satisfaction of the slayer of Madhu. / This glorification of the month of Mādhava has been declared to you,
as was formerly heard by me from the mouth of Brahmā, O King.

5.87.m: Sūta said: / Having heard those words of Nārada, the king, / having bowed, spoke with astonishment, meditating in his mind upon Hari:
Ambarīṣa said: / How is this, O sage? We are bewildered that through little exertion / an exceedingly rare fruit is attained merely by bathing.
Nārada said: / It is true, O King, what you say: that great fruit is attained / with little exertion; in that matter, have faith in the teaching of the ordinances.
The ways of dharma are subtle and difficult to comprehend even by rulers; / the learned too are bewildered here, for the power of Hari's action is inconceivable.
Viśvāmitra and others, O King, though born from the arms [as kṣatriyas], attained brāhmaṇahood / through an abundance of dharma; therefore the way of dharma is subtle.
Even Ajāmila, O King, is renowned as the husband of a maidservant, / an abandoner of his lawful wife, who was constantly stationed on the path of sin.
While dying, out of affection for his son he uttered 'Nārāyaṇa', / and through meditating on him and taking his name, he attained a most difficult-to-reach abode.
Just as fire burns when touched even unintentionally, / so the name of Govinda burns [away sin] even when spoken under a pretext.
The grandsons of the sage born to an unmarried girl, who cohabited with their brother's wife; / the sons of Pāṇḍu, born of a widow, and themselves born of adultery—
all five of them, O King, the Pāṇḍavas devoted to Draupadī, / are renowned for their holy fame; therefore the way of dharma is subtle.
Varied are actions, and varied are the thoughts of living beings; / varied are the beings, and varied are the powers of actions.
Sometimes a virtuous action that remains dormant / increases, O King, on account of some auspicious deed;
it gives a very great fruit in some birth or other. / Dharma is subtle and deeply unfathomable; it cannot be measured simply as this or that.
No absolute certainty regarding the bestowal of its fruit is known, O King. / Whatever little virtuous deed there is, even though covered by other sins,
comes from somewhere at some time and bestows its own fruit. / There is no destruction in this world of merit or sin that has been performed.
Even so, terrible sin departs through numerous merits. / As for what was said by you, O king, that [the result] must correspond to the magnitude of exertion,
from an abundance of exertion, hear the reason from me on that point: / If slightness and greatness [of merit] depended on slight exertion and great exertion,
then plowmen and others would constantly possess great merit; / for chanting a mantra involves little effort, whereas the exertion of a lion and other beasts is great.
The praised five cow-products indeed would not constitute a limb of a vow, / nor would an abundance of duties [constitute] greatness, nor the smallness thereof;
entering fire, water, and so on might be enjoined for another vow. / 'This is small, and this is great'—this is not the determinant at all.
Whatever fruit is enjoined in scripture, that alone would be great, O king. / Just as the small is destroyed by the great, so the great is destroyed by the small;
for even by a tiny spark a heap of grass is burnt away.
Ten thousand murders, a thousand terrible sins, cohabitation with a million wives of gurus, / and sins like theft born of ignorance are taken to destruction by devotees of Kṛṣṇa.
O hero, whatever small meritorious deed is performed / by a wise person possessing devotion to Viṣṇu, he obtains imperishable fruit from it.
No doubt should be harbored here: by worshiping Mādhava in the month of Mādhava / with devotion, a man attains whatever he desires.
Offspring, wealth, jewels, wives, palaces, horses, elephants, / pleasures, heaven, and liberation are not far off through devotion to Hari.
Thus, by the method taught in scripture, even by a very small deed—there is no doubt— / there will be destruction of even great sin and an increase of good deeds.
The superiority of the fruit comes from the superiority of one's inner disposition and actions, O king. / The course of dharma is to be known as subtle even through various ways.
This month of Mādhava is dear to the great-souled Mādhava. / Even a single [observance] performed by people bestows all desires.
O king, one devoted to bathing in holy Gaṅgā water at [the proper] time and place, / even if a giver, if devoid of right disposition from birth, does not attain purity; such is my view.

Living beings abide constantly at holy places like the Gaṅgā, and flocks of birds in a temple; / though having fasted, they meet destruction, and lacking devotion, they do not attain a good destination at all.
Therefore, placing his disposition in the heart-lotus, he who, pure and intent on bathing, / worships glorious Mādhava with devotion in the month of Mādhava—we are not able to describe his merit.

Even if one enters a fire fed with ghee and oil, having flames curling to the right, and is burned at the proper time, / if corrupted in intention, he indeed attains neither heaven nor any other fruit.
Therefore, O king, have faith regarding the fruit of Mādhava. / Even a very small auspicious deed destroys hundreds of bad actions.
Just as all the hosts of sins are destroyed by fear of Hari's name, O king, / so indeed, when the sun has entered Aries, at dawn, through bathing at a holy place and through praise of Hari,
sins flee like serpents before the brilliance of the son of Vinatā / through bathing at dawn in Vaiśākha—this is certain.
Having bathed in the Gaṅgā or the Narmadā when the sun has entered Aries, / whoever recites the sin-quelling hymn with devotional disposition,
once a day, twice, or at all three twilights, O king, / he goes to the supreme abode, freed from all sins.
O Ambarīṣa, undertake the observation for the attainment of great merit: / bathing indeed in the morning in the month of Mādhava, steadfast in vows.
What is spoken of for those residing for ten million years in Ānartapura, / that is obtained by a single morning bath in the month of Mādhava.
In this regard, listen to what happened of old, O king: / the conversation of the twice-born Devaśarman with his wife.
On the holy bank of the Revā, at the holy ford of Amarakaṇṭaka, / Devaśarman, the best among the twice-born, was born as the son of Kauśika.
Bereft of wealth and sons, accompanied by much sorrow, / he was always afflicted by terrible poverty and grief.
Day and night he would brood upon the means to obtain wealth and a son. / Then one day, his beloved wife, Sumanā by name, true to her vows,
noticed her husband filled with anxiety, his face turned down. / Seeing her husband then, that illustrious woman said to him:
"Your mind is dragged down by countless nets of sorrow. / You are bewildered by delusion; cast off anxiety, O highly intelligent one!
Speak your grief to me; become calm and find happiness. / There is no sorrow like anxiety, which merely dries up the body.
Abandoning it, one should act, and he rejoices in happiness. / Tell me the cause of your anxiety, O master, O brāhmaṇa!"
Nārada said: / Having heard the words of his beloved wife, that highly intelligent Devaśarman, / the companion of a virtuous wife, though distressed, pleased, spoke these words:
Devaśarman said: / "O blessed lady, whatever cause of grief has been contemplated by you, / I shall explain all of that; listen and understand it.
I do not know through what sin I am devoid of wealth, O lady of good vows, / and likewise I am bereft of a son. This is the cause of my grief."
Sumanā said: / "Listen, I shall proclaim the destruction of all doubt, / the essential nature of instruction, the vision of all knowledge.
Contentment alone is the supreme merit, the cause of happiness and the like; / discontent is the supreme sin—so said the blessed Lord Hari.
Greed is this seed of sin, and delusion is indeed its root; / falsehood is its trunk, with great branches stretching wide;
pride and crookedness are its leaves; it is ever in flower through wicked intellect; / untruth is its fragrance, and ignorance is its fruit;
and walls, heretics, thieves, the cruel, deceitful, and sinful / are the birds perched on the great branches of this tree of delusion.
Ignorance is its fine fruit, unrighteousness is the juice of that fruit; / it is nourished by the water of inner feeling, and its faith is fond of rituals;
its sap is in unrighteous deeds, made sweet by foul discharges; / and with such fruits, the tree of greed is bearing fruit.
Whatever man goes about taking shelter in its shade, / he eats its self-ripened fruits day after day.
Nourished by unrighteousness through the juice of those fruits, / that mortal, grown plump, heads toward a fall.
Therefore, laying aside anxiety, my lord should not harbor greed; / he should not harbor this worry over wealth, sons, and wives.
If a wise man does not [guard himself], O beloved, he indeed takes the path of fools; / he constantly worries in vain, bewildered day and night:
'And for an auspicious purpose I obtain—how may I get sons?' / Thus he constantly broods, bewildered day and night.
For a single moment he may see great happiness in the midst of anxiety, / then returns to consciousness, and is afflicted with great sorrow.
Abandoning anxiety and delusion, follow that [truth], O twice-born! / In this transmigratory world, there is no [permanent] connection with anyone, O highly intelligent one!
Friends, kinsmen, sons, father, mother, and daughters— / these exist due to one's own karmic bond, and wives and the rest likewise."
Devaśarman said: / "What kind of connection is that, O blessed lady? Tell me that in detail, / by which all those wealth, sons, and kinsmen are born."
Sumanā said: / "O husband, sons are born in five ways; I will declare them: / one is the stealer of a deposit, another is related by debt,
an enemy, an advantageous one, and an indifferent one—so they are, O beloved. / I shall describe their characteristics separately, O lord.
Sons, friends, beloved wives, fathers, mothers, and kinsmen / are indeed born on the earth according to their own respective connections.
By whomsoever anything was taken on earth by way of misappropriating a deposit, / the owner of that deposit becomes a virtuous and handsome son on earth.
In the house of the one by whom a deposit was stolen, no doubt, / having given terrible grief over the theft of that deposit, he departed.
The owner of the deposit became an excellent son to that thief of the deposit, / endowed with virtues and handsome, equipped with all auspicious marks.
Having become a son, he would show devotion to him day by day; / speaking sweetly, pleasant-voiced, eloquent, he would show great affection.
Having recovered his own wealth and generated peerless love, / just as after the theft of the deposit that was given by him,
terrible, life-destroying grief of such a kind, O fortunate one, / having become a son endowed with great virtues, he gives to him.
Thus becoming short-lived, he meets with death; / having thus given grief, having struck him again and again, he departs.
When he laments, crying, “O son! O son!”, / then this one laughs: “Who is whose son?”
“By this evil-doer my deposit was stolen; / through the theft of that wealth my life was indeed lost,
with great and unbearable grief formerly; / so now, having given grief, the excellent wealth has been reclaimed by me.”

5.88.m: Sumanā said: / I shall describe before you a son connected through debt; / having taken whose debt one indeed meets death,
that giver of wealth, having become a son, a brother, a father, or a beloved wife, / would live in the guise of a friend, but always wicked inside.
Cruel, of harsh appearance, he would never see any virtue; / he always speaks harsh words among his own relatives.
He eats only the sweetest foods and constantly enjoys pleasures; / always devoted to gambling, he has a craving for theft.
He steals wealth from the house, and when restrained, he gets angry; / and he reviles his father and mother day by day.
Wealth is thus destroyed, and he even says this: / “The house, the fields, and all else are mine alone, without a doubt.”
He indeed harms his father and mother day by day, / with heavy sticks and pestles, and by pulling their hair cruelly.
And when that father and mother are dead, he is exceedingly harsh; / he becomes loveless and cruel, of this there is no doubt.
He never performs the ancestral rites or gifts; / such are the dear sons that exist, O king.
I shall describe an enemy-son before you, O best of twice-born: / when childhood is reached, he always remains in the condition of a son.
While playing, he strikes both his father and his mother; / having struck them, he goes away, laughing again and again.
He comes back there again to the father and mother; / he is always full of wrath and reviles them day by day.
Thus he always conducts himself completely in acts of hostility; / having beaten his father and then again his mother,
that wicked-minded one departs in this way, through the power of former enmity. / Now, next, I shall describe how an affectionate [son] may be obtained.
As soon as he is born he gives pleasure; in childhood by games and playful striking; / having attained youth, he brings joy thereafter to his mother and father.
He constantly satisfies them with devotion; he gladdens them both / with affection, with words, and with affectionate conversation.
When his two elders have died, he weeps again out of affection; / [he performs] all the ancestral rites and the ritual of offering funeral balls.
Afflicted with deep grief, he indeed performs [them]; he undertakes pilgrimages for them; / and bound by the three debts, he surely frees them out of affection.
From whom a reward is due, O dear one, he gives it, without doubt, / having become a son in this manner, O very wise one.
I will now speak before you of an indifferent one, O dear one: / he always behaves with a disposition of indifference.
He neither gives nor takes, nor does he get angry or satisfied; / he does not go away abandoning them, being indifferent, O best of twice-born.
Servants are also declared as such, and so are beasts, horses, / elephants, she-buffaloes, and female slaves: these are bound by debt.
If only one took [what was his] through illusion, neither of us owes anything to anyone; / for no deposit was indeed made to anyone in a previous life.
I do not propitiate anyone, even for a moment, beloved—listen indeed! / Nor was hostility ever committed against anyone in a past life.
From my childhood, O best of Brahmins, I have never abandoned my husband. / Knowing this, attain peace and abandon useless anxiety.
Nothing at all was stolen from anyone, nor was anything given back by you. / How then could wealth come to you? Do not be astonished, O lord!
Indeed, whatever is obtained does not remain with one who merely tries to guard it. / Knowing this, attain peace and abandon useless anxiety.
Whose sons are they? Whose beloved wife? Whose kinsmen and relatives? / Who belongs to whom in worldly existence? There is no real connection, O best of Brahmins.
Deluded by the illusion of infatuation, humans of sinful mind think: / 'This is my house, this is my son, this is my wife.'
Untrue is seen the bond of worldly existence, O beloved!

5.89.m: Nārada said: / Thus addressed, the Brahmin Devaśarman, best of the twice-born, / again spoke to his beloved wife, who was endowed with wisdom:
Truth has been spoken by you, auspicious lady, destroying all doubts; / nevertheless, virtuous and truly wise people desire a lineage.
My anxiety is not so much for wealth, O beloved, as it is for a son. / By whatever means possible, I will father a son.
Sumanā said: / Through a son one conquers worlds; a son delivers the family line. / Through a good son, O highly fortunate one, father and mother thrive.
One son is superior, beloved; what is the use of many devoid of virtue? / One delivers the lineage, while the others cause distress.
As I have already said, others merely share in worldly bonds. / A son is obtained through merit; a lineage is obtained through merit.
A good conception is obtained through merits, and a wretched death through sins, / as well as an accumulation of pleasures, beloved—truly indeed I speak.
By celibacy, by truth, by ascetic heat, by constant righteous practices, / by charity, and by observances, by forbearance and purity, O dear one,
and by non-violence according to one's capacity, and even by non-stealing one proceeds: / through these ten limbs, dharma is thus brought forth.
Dharma is born complete in its limbs, just as an embryo in the womb. / The virtuous person generates dharma by three kinds of action alone.
Dharma, pleased in spirit, grants him meritorious happiness; / whatever the wise person contemplates, that rare [fruit] he obtains.
Devaśarman said: / Everything has been explained by you, O lady, this supreme knowledge called dharma. / How may I obtain a son who is a Vaiṣṇava, endowed with virtues?
Tell me, O highly fortunate one, if you know, O woman of virtuous vows. / The entire path of dharma was obtained by you from your father formerly, O sinless one.
This is known to me, O beloved: you are an expounder of the Veda, / through the grace of Cyavana, and of Viṣṇu who was pleased with you formerly.
Sumanā said: / Go to Vasiṣṭha, O knower of dharma, and pray to that great sage; / from him you will obtain a son who knows dharma and is fond of dharma.
When this speech was uttered by her, Devaśarman, best of the twice-born, [said]: / 'I shall act according to your auspicious opinion; there is no doubt.'
Having spoken thus, that Devaśarman, best of the twice-born, went / to Vasiṣṭha, the all-knowing, radiant, best among practitioners of ascetic heat,
the meritorious, best of the twice-born seated on a seat on the bank of the Gaṅgā, / enveloped in blazing splendor like a second sun,
the shining, great-souled lion among Brahmins, best of the twice-born. / Bowing with devotion to that sage like a staff again and again,
the son of Brahmā of great splendor spoke to him who was free of impurity: / 'Sit down comfortably on a holy seat, O highly intelligent one!'
Nārada said: / Seated, that lord of yogins spoke again to the rich in ascetic heat: / 'O child, in your home, among your wife and servants, is there always'
welfare, O highly fortunate one, and in your meritorious rites and sacred fires? / Are you free from disease in your limbs, and do you always preserve dharma?'
Having spoken thus, the highly wise one said again to the earthly god: / 'What desired and very pleasing favor may I do for you, O best of Brahmins?'
Nārada said: / Having thus addressed the Brahmin, his auspicious speech ceased. / Then the highly fortunate Brahmin [spoke] to Vasiṣṭha, the foremost of sages.
He spoke to the great-souled Vasiṣṭha, the best among practitioners of ascetic heat: / 'O venerable one, let my words be heard; resolve [this doubt], O best of Brahmins!
From what cause does poverty arise, and why is there no happiness from a son? / This is my doubt, O father; tell me, from what sin [does this come]?
Bewildered by great delusion, I was instructed by my beloved, O twice-born one. / Sent by her, O father, I have come to your presence.
Explain all that, which destroys all doubt; / become the giver of liberation for me from the bond of worldly existence.'
Vasiṣṭha said: / Sons, friends, a brother, and other relatives and kinsmen: / these are the five kinds of relationships that exist for a man.
These were already explained to you previously by Sumanā; / all those related by debt are bad sons, O best of Brahmins.
I shall explain before you the meritorious characteristic of a son: / one whose self is attached to merit, who is always devoted to truth and dharma,
pure, endowed with knowledge, practicing ascetic heat, the best of eloquent speakers, / dedicated to all proper duties, devoted to Vedic recitation,
fully knowledgeable in all scriptures, a worshipper of gods and Brahmins, / a sacrificer in all sacrifices, generous, renouncing, speaking pleasantly,
always devoted to meditating on Viṣṇu, calm, self-controlled, always a good friend, / constantly devoted to his father and mother, affectionate to all his kinsmen,
a savior of the family line, learned, nourishing his own lineage— / endowed with such virtues, a good son is a giver of happiness.
Others, bound by mere relationships, cause grief and distress. / What use have you for an indifferent [son] who bears no fruit, O sinless one?
They come and they go, all having given terribly harsh sorrow, / all of them in the form of sons in worldly existence, O best of Brahmins.
The action performed in a previous life that was maintained by you: / I shall tell you all of that; listen again to this wonder!
You were a Śūdra, O highly intelligent one, in a previous life—not otherwise; / a farmer, devoid of knowledge, endowed with great greed,
having one wife, always malicious, having many sons, never giving; / you did not know dharma or established truth at all.
No gift was given by you, no scripture was listened to, / no sacred ford was visited by you, nor any pilgrimage, O highly intelligent one.
Thus the path of agriculture was pursued by you again and again, O Brahmin; / in the past, while walking along, O best of the twice-born, you tended livestock;
tending buffaloes and mares again and again: / such was the deed done in the past by you, O best of Brahmins.
Vast wealth, likewise, was amassed out of greed; / but its expenditure for merit was never made by you.
No gift was given to a worthy recipient, even on seeing him weak; / having practiced agriculture, no wealth was given by you.
Selling all this cow-dung and the yield of the livestock, / vast wealth was accumulated by you, O Brahmin.
Buttermilk, ghee, and milk, and curds were constantly sold [by you]; / famine was anticipated, O twice-born, deluded by the illusion of Viṣṇu.
Making this wealth extremely expensive, O best of brāhmaṇas, / ruthless as you were, no gift was given by you at that time.
Worship of the gods was never performed by you, O twice-born; / reaching auspicious festival days, no wealth was offered to brāhmaṇas.
And when the time for ancestral rites arrived, it was not performed by you with faith; / your virtuous wife said, when the midday had arrived:
“It is the time for the ancestral rites of your father-in-law and mother-in-law, O highly intelligent one!” / Hearing that speech of hers, you would flee, abandoning the house.
The path of dharma was never seen or heard of at any time by you; / greed was your mother, father, and brother; greed was your kin and relatives.
Greed alone was cherished, having always abandoned dharma; / therefore you have become miserable, exceedingly afflicted by poverty.
Day by day a great craving arose in your heart; / whenever wealth increased in your house, then
burned by craving having the form of fire, / or sleeping at night, you thought only of more greed.
Reaching daytime, you were always pervaded by great delusions: / “When will there be a thousand, a hundred thousand, ten million, or even a hundred million,
when will ten billion and a hundred billion be in my house?” / Thus a thousand, a hundred thousand, ten million, a hundred million,
ten billion, and a hundred billion were gathered, yet the craving never departed; / thus, wasting time, it grew continually.
Nothing was ever given or offered in sacrifice by you, O twice-born, nor was it ever enjoyed; / it was placed securely inside the earth, and your sons did not know.
You constantly adopted other means for the sake of the arrival of wealth, O twice-born; / wise as you were, you questioned people.
Asking about magical spades, salves, transmutation, and alchemy beyond that, / you wandered alone, utterly deluded by craving.
You constantly pondered all the rituals that bestow supernatural accomplishments; / you asked about the penetration of variegated colors and the wish-fulfilling jewel.
Burned by the fire of craving, you attain no happiness; / inflamed by the fire of craving, you became lamenting and senseless.
Being such, O leader of twice-born, you fell under the control of time. / When that wealth was asked about by your wife and sons,
it was not revealed, nor was it given; abandoning your life breaths, you went to Yama. / Thus your whole past history has been told by me.
By this action, O twice-born, you have become destitute and poor. / In this world, the one whose sons are good, always possessing devotion,
virtuous, endowed with knowledge, and always devoted to truth and dharma, / are born in his house when Viṣṇu is pleased with him.
Wealth, grain, a wife, and endless sons and grandsons / he enjoys in the mortal world, when Viṣṇu is gracious to him.
Without the grace of Viṣṇu, a wife and sons do not come to be, / nor good birth in a family, O twice-born; that is the supreme state of Viṣṇu.
